shows.description:
Joel-Peter Witkin has spent five decades building elaborately staged photographs that look like they were unearthed from some forgotten wing of art history — tableaux populated by cadavers, amputees, hermaphrodites, and other figures excluded from conventional pictures of beauty, arranged with the same compositional seriousness Velázquez or Goya brought to a royal court. This survey, pulling together prints from 1974 through 2018, traces how consistent that vision has been: the theatrical backdrops, the scratched and toned negatives, the constant citation of old-master painting even as the subject matter refuses every one of its comforts.

What makes the work more than shock value is the craft underneath it. Witkin doesn't just photograph his tableaux — he attacks the negative and print afterward, scratching the emulsion, bleaching sections, sometimes drawing directly on the surface, so that each finished piece sits somewhere between photograph and hand-worked object. The pictures reference Picasso, Courbet, and Christian iconography as often as they reference the darkroom, and the effect is a body of work that treats mortality and the marginalized body as subjects worthy of the grandest possible visual language.

Fahey/Klein has spent nearly forty years as one of the country's foremost photography galleries, and this show is a fitting anniversary gesture: a chance to see a genuinely singular, still-controversial photographic practice presented with the scholarly care usually reserved for painting retrospectives.

spans.text: Fahey/Klein has spent nearly forty years as one of the country's foremost photography galleries

shows.description:
Small Hours brings together five artists whose work has each, in different ways, built substantial international reputations — Cyprien Gaillard, Farah Al Qasimi, Kang Seung Lee, P. Staff, and Torbjørn Rødland — for a closing-week group show at Canary Test, the scrappy nonprofit gallery and event space that's become one of the more interesting fixtures of the Arts District's project-space scene. The title points to a liminal register: works that operate in dim, in-between light, whether emotional, temporal, or literal.

Given the range of practices involved — Gaillard's found-footage and site-specific interventions, Al Qasimi's staged photography, Lee's work threading queer history and diasporic memory, Staff's visceral moving image and sculpture, Rødland's uncanny studio photography — the show reads less as a thematic thesis than as a curated conversation between artists who share an interest in atmosphere over statement.

Canary Test operates as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit with a genuinely experimental program, mixing gallery exhibitions with its Canary Sound Werk music series, and this show is a good entry point for anyone who hasn't caught the space before — it's only up through September 2, so this is a last-chance visit.

spans.text: the scrappy nonprofit gallery and event space that's become one of the more interesting fixtures of the Arts District's project-space scene
Canary Test operates as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit with a genuinely experimental program, mixing gallery exhibitions with its Canary Sound Werk music series

shows.description:
"Object Poetry" gathers artists who treat sculpture and assemblage as a kind of compressed language, where everyday materials and cast-off objects are recombined until they start to read like verse. The checklist spans generations and temperaments: Bruce Conner's uncanny assemblage sensibility sits alongside Tony Oursler's video-inflected sculptures, large-scale photographic works, and pieces that play with domestic scale and architectural miniature. Across the two galleries, the through-line is a fascination with objecthood itself — the way a chair leg, a lens, or a scrap of fabric can carry more meaning once it's pulled out of use and set into a composition.

Michael Kohn Gallery has spent four decades building relationships with exactly this kind of artist — people who use assemblage, collage, and sculptural accumulation to talk about memory, media, and the residue of everyday life. Seeing the works installed together across the gallery's two main rooms makes clear how much these different practices share: a belief that objects, arranged with enough attention, behave like sentences.

This is a good show for anyone who likes sculpture that rewards close looking — pieces built from many small decisions rather than one big gesture. It's on view concurrently with a solo survey of Mark Innerst's paintings in the gallery's third room, making a visit worth the time for two very different but complementary shows under one roof.

spans.text: Michael Kohn Gallery has spent four decades building relationships with exactly this kind of artist — people who use assemblage, collage, and sculptural accumulation to talk about memory, media, and the residue of everyday life.

shows.description:
Alfredo Ramos Martínez is often called the father of Mexican Modernism — he mentored David Alfaro Siqueiros and Rufino Tamayo and pushed a generation of painters out of the studio and into the landscape. This exhibition, drawn from the artist's estate (which Louis Stern Fine Arts exclusively represents), gathers tempera-on-paper and oil landscapes made after his 1929 move to Los Angeles, when homesickness for Mexico's mountains and markets became a lifelong subject.

The show's anchor works trace a single mental thread: the Cordillera, the mountain spine that runs from the Sierra Madre down through the Americas. Martínez's Cordillera Mexicana pays tribute to the Sierra Madre Oriental peaks above his native Monterrey, while other paintings place indigenous women bearing flowers and produce beneath the volcanoes ringing the Valley of Mexico. Even his delicate studies of floripondio blossoms — a South American flower he found growing as an ornamental in both Mexico and Southern California — read as a metaphor for his own transplanted life.

It's a quieter, more historical show than most of what's on view in LA's contemporary-leaning galleries right now, but a good one for anyone curious about the roots of Mexican modernism as seen from Los Angeles, a city where Martínez spent his final two decades and where his legacy is held in depth at LACMA and beyond.

spans.text: which Louis Stern Fine Arts exclusively represents

shows.description:
Roger Herman has been a fixture of Los Angeles painting since the late 1970s, and this show finds the German-born, UCLA-affiliated artist doing what he does best: turning flowers, mountains, and skulls into loose, saturated fields of brushwork that refuse to sit still. The poppy paintings are the emotional center — layered, almost gaudy stacks of leaf and petal built from dashes and smears rather than careful description — while a companion landscape painting renders a mountain in broad strokes of blue, turquoise, and white.

What makes the show more than a painting survey is the ceramics. Herman throws large, irregular vessels on the wheel and then treats the glazing the way he treats a canvas, letting color pool and shift unpredictably across the surface. A dining table and coffee table extend that same logic into furniture, their tops built from painterly ceramic panels, and a set of tiny mezcal cups modeled on the traditional jicara round out the display at a much more intimate scale.

Carpenters Workshop Gallery is best known internationally for design-forward, collectible objects, and pairing that program with an untidy, expressionist painter like Herman is a smart bit of counter-programming — proof that the gallery's West Hollywood outpost isn't just showing polished design pieces but also giving space to an artist whose work resists polish on principle.

spans.text: Carpenters Workshop Gallery is best known internationally for design-forward, collectible objects

shows.description:
Organized by Aram Moshayedi with a circle of Iranian curators, writers, and artists as consultants, this group exhibition grew out of an unusual constraint: the works on view were conceived through proposals, instructions, and letters sent by artists living and working inside Iran, then physically realized by other artists and collaborators acting as their proxies. The project took shape in the shadow of specific, recent crisis — daily bombardment and an extended nationwide internet blackout — conditions that made direct authorship and even ordinary communication impossible for the artists who originated the ideas.

The result is less a conventional survey than a study in transmission and trust: what happens to an artwork when the hand that finishes it is not the mind that conceived it. The Brick's installation photographs suggest a spare, deliberately unresolved installation, appropriate to a show built on incomplete information and long-distance instruction rather than finished objects arriving intact.

It's a timely, quietly political exhibition from an artist-run nonprofit that has consistently used its Western Avenue space to platform work that commercial galleries are unlikely to take on, and it rewards visitors willing to read wall text and press materials as carefully as the art itself.

spans.text: from an artist-run nonprofit that has consistently used its Western Avenue space to platform work that commercial galleries are unlikely to take on

shows.description:
Taix French Restaurant sat on Sunset Boulevard in Echo Park for nearly a century before it closed and was gutted for redevelopment, and this show is essentially six photographers and one mixed-media artist working through what that kind of loss looks like. Maxfield Hegedus shot the interior room by room before demolition — bar, ballroom, dining room, both bathrooms, the private room — turning a beloved but unglamorous restaurant into a document of a particular strain of mid-century LA design. Abdi Taslimi's acrylic-laminated photographs of the dining room and the Rhône Room work a similar vein in a different register, more saturated and object-like on their aluminum mounts.

The show nods explicitly to Ed Ruscha's "Every Building on the Sunset Strip," and that reference gives the whole project its logic: this is vernacular architecture photography as elegy, cataloguing a stretch of the city's built environment right before it disappears. Evan Whale's altered c-print, carved and chemigrammed until the image partially dissolves into smoke and texture, is the most physically worked-over piece in the show and a good counterpoint to the more straightforward documentary images around it.

Gallery Luisotti has spent decades as one of LA's steadiest venues for landscape and documentary photography, and this show fits that mission precisely — using a single closed restaurant as a lens onto memory, urban change, and the particular melancholy of watching a familiar place get erased.

spans.text: Gallery Luisotti has spent decades as one of LA's steadiest venues for landscape and documentary photography

shows.description:
Matthew Grabelsky is best known for dropping wide-eyed animal-headed figures — his signature mash-up of human bodies and cartoon or animal faces — into the fluorescent-lit purgatory of the New York subway. "Kiddos" narrows that lens to childhood: playground scuffles, temper tantrums, sibling rivalries, and the small dramas of growing up, all rendered with the same uncanny, hyper-real polish he brings to his transit paintings.

The effect is somewhere between Norman Rockwell and a fever dream — technically dazzling figurative painting that uses its animal-headed cast to sidestep easy sentimentality about childhood. A kid mid-tantrum or a "cool kid" in a playground standoff reads as funnier and stranger with a fox or rabbit head than it would with an ordinary human face, and Grabelsky clearly knows it.

Thinkspace has spent two decades championing exactly this kind of pop-surrealist, illustration-adjacent painting, and Grabelsky's meticulous, faintly melancholic style is a good fit for a gallery that treats craft and narrative as virtues rather than liabilities.

spans.text: Thinkspace has spent two decades championing exactly this kind of pop-surrealist, illustration-adjacent painting, and Grabelsky's meticulous, faintly melancholic style is a good fit for a gallery that treats craft and narrative as virtues rather than liabilities.

shows.description:
Tiger Strikes Asteroid's Los Angeles outpost turns its project space over to a loose coalition of artists, journalists and activists for this six-person show built around a single question: what do we owe the things we witness? Curated by TSA-LA member Fatemeh Burnes, the exhibition treats photography, sculpture, installation, painting and performance documentation as different tools for the same job — holding a mirror up to conflict, migration and injustice without pretending to resolve them.

The roster mixes practicing photojournalists with studio artists, which gives the show an unusual friction. Sahab Zaribaf, an Iranian-born photographer whose images have run through Getty and AFP, contributes press-honed images of moments that resist tidy narratives. Mei Xian Qiu's scroll-and-puppet installation Angel Island revisits the poetry Chinese detainees etched into the walls of the Angel Island immigration station, while Guatemalan-born, LA-based Maria Adela Diaz brings her body-centered performance practice to bear on questions of patriarchy and displacement. Sculptor Mary Linda Moss and painter Michal Greenfield work in more interior registers, using organic materials and portraiture to trace how history and trauma settle into the body.

It's a modest, artist-run show rather than a blockbuster, but that's exactly the TSA model: a nonprofit network of self-curated spaces that gives working artists room to test out hard, unresolved ideas. Worth a visit for anyone interested in how contemporary art is grappling with journalism's crisis of authority and the ethics of looking.

spans.text: that's exactly the TSA model: a nonprofit network of self-curated spaces that gives working artists room to test out hard, unresolved ideas

shows.description:
Words Matter gathers seventeen artists from Tierra del Sol's studio program around a single, deceptively simple question: what happens when text itself becomes the material of art? The gallery, which represents artists with developmental disabilities as part of the Tierra del Sol Foundation, turns its walls over to visitors as well — the show invites people to write, draw, and tag directly on the gallery walls, turning the exhibition into a growing collective mural over its run.

Among the standouts are Leon Fuller, a longtime Tierra artist since the late 1990s whose text-and-drawing works pull from mass media and celebrity culture, and Joe Zaldivar, whose fictional advertisements mimic real brands while subverting their language. Mary Lou Dimsdale contributes electric, mosaic-toned pieces built from scavenged news text. A sound piece, Exquisite Dream, stitches together studio artists' recorded dream accounts into one collaborative audio work playing in the gallery's Annex, echoing the show's larger interest in voice, collectivity, and what gets said versus what gets silenced.

It's a rare kind of group show — genuinely interactive, unpretentious about its methods, and a useful reminder that outsider and disability-inclusive art spaces in LA are producing some of the city's most inventive text-based work right now.

spans.text: The gallery, which represents artists with developmental disabilities as part of the Tierra del Sol Foundation,

shows.description:
JAPAN HOUSE Los Angeles turns its second-floor gallery over to food itself with WASHOKU, an exhibition exploring the UNESCO-listed culinary tradition of washoku — Japan's rice-and-fish-centered cuisine and its deep entanglement with the archipelago's climate, seasons, and history. Developed with Tokyo's National Museum of Nature and Science and The Asahi Shimbun, this is the show's first presentation outside Japan, and it leans on the kind of hybrid display JAPAN HOUSE does well: natural history specimens, food replicas, historical meal reconstructions, and interactive multimedia rather than paintings on a wall.

The show is organized into five sections that move from a basic question — what is washoku, really? — through the ingredients unique to Japan's geography, a long historical arc from the Jōmon period through the postwar era, the tools and techniques that define the cuisine's precision, and finally washoku's globalization, sushi included. Along the way there are replica meal settings (including a reconstruction of an eighth-century aristocratic banquet from the Nara National Research Institute for Cultural Properties), specimens of fish and vegetables, and archival ephemera like period cookbooks and manga panels.

It's less an art exhibition in the conventional sense than a design- and culture-focused installation, which is exactly the kind of programming JAPAN HOUSE has made its niche inside the Hollywood tourist corridor. Free admission and a steady rotation of related talks and tastings make it an easy, family-friendly stop for anyone curious about the deeper logic behind Japanese food culture.

spans.text: it leans on the kind of hybrid display JAPAN HOUSE does well
which is exactly the kind of programming JAPAN HOUSE has made its niche inside the Hollywood tourist corridor

shows.description:
Shen Yongji's first U.S. solo show is a study in what happens when an ancient Chinese decorative technique gets rebuilt with entirely modern materials. Working in acrylic, crystal resin, gold, and silver, Shen builds sculptural, light-catching structures out of slices, grids, and layered translucent panels — forms that owe their logic to cuo jin yin, the historic craft of inlaying gold and silver into a surface, but that have none of the weight or opacity of traditional metalwork.

The results read as objects built for looking through as much as looking at: light bends and scatters across their sliced and matrixed surfaces, so a piece changes as a viewer moves around it, shifting between transparency, reflection, and color. That responsiveness to light and to the viewer's position is clearly intentional — Shen is less interested in material as symbol than in material as something that keeps producing new visual information as circumstances (light, angle, attention) change around it.

The show is a good fit for H Foundation's stated mission of connecting contemporary practice to Asian and diasporic craft traditions without turning that history into ornament — here, the inherited technique is a starting point for new sculptural language rather than something being simply preserved or referenced.

spans.text: The show is a good fit for H Foundation's stated mission of connecting contemporary practice to Asian and diasporic craft traditions without turning that history into ornament

shows.description:
Helena Reis's first mini-solo at Copro Gallery gathers six small works on wood panel, each about a foot square, built up with watercolor pencil, watercolor, acrylic, gouache and gold leaf. The Lisbon-based artist paints a private bestiary of hooded figures, birds and half-human creatures rendered in a palette of dusky blues and warm ochres — imagery she's described as balancing something creepy and cute in equal measure.

The small scale and mixed-media layering give the paintings the feel of illuminated manuscript pages or storybook illustrations gone slightly feral. Reis has said the work grew out of turning her own fears and nightmares into something she could look at directly, even find humor in — a kind of exposure therapy carried out one gilded, moody little panel at a time.

It's a quiet, densely worked counterpoint to the bigger, brasher shows Copro is known for, worth a close look on the same visit as Mook Simpson's "America Dreaming" and Dale Sizer's mini-show, both hanging concurrently in the same space.

spans.text: the bigger, brasher shows Copro is known for

shows.description:
Mook Simpson paints over reproductions of 19th-century American frontier paintings — Bierstadt, Remington, Charles Marion Russell, George Caleb Bingham — inserting bronco-riding tentacled creatures, alien visitors, and other invasive oddities into the found Western tableaux. The effect is a sly, cartoonish vandalism of Manifest Destiny iconography: the same wagon trains and buffalo hunts that once mythologized the American frontier are recast as sites of strange visitation, undercutting their heroic tone with pulp-comic humor.

The show runs alongside solo presentations by Helena Reis and Dale Sizer in Copro's other rooms. Reis contributes small, jewel-toned panels — gold leaf, oil and acrylic renderings of birds and winged figures rendered with a devotional, illuminated-manuscript intensity that plays well against Simpson's rowdier revisionism next door.

Copro has been a fixture at Bergamot Station since 1999, championing lowbrow and pop-surrealist painting, and this triple bill is typical of its monthly rotating format: dense hangs of affordable, narrative-driven work aimed as much at collectors of illustration and comics as at gallery regulars.

spans.text: Copro has been a fixture at Bergamot Station since 1999, championing lowbrow and pop-surrealist painting, and this triple bill is typical of its monthly rotating format: dense hangs of affordable, narrative-driven work aimed as much at collectors of illustration and comics as at gallery regulars.

shows.description:
KP Projects pairs two Brazilian painters for late summer, each working a very different register of hyper-saturated realism. Rafael Silveira's Popsicledelic Trip leans into candy-colored, almost hallucinatory still lifes and figures — surfaces so glossy and lit they read like renderings of a sugar rush, with titles ("Visual Mantra," "Wonders of Human Nature") that hint at a wry, semi-spiritual undercurrent beneath the pop sheen.

Flávia Itiberê's Pause works in a quieter but equally intense key, built around close studies of single figures and objects — a mask-like face, a wrapped or held object — rendered with the same airbrushed precision but pulled back into stillness rather than trip-like excess. Placed side by side, the two bodies of work argue for hyperreal technique as a vehicle for two opposite moods: one accelerant, one suspended.

KP Projects has long been a home for pop surrealism and figurative painting on La Brea, and this two-hander is a solid entry point into that scene — vivid, technically showy work that photographs well but rewards a slow look in person for the airbrush-level detail.

spans.text: KP Projects has long been a home for pop surrealism and figurative painting on La Brea

shows.description:
Moth To A Flame is a collaborative installation by the artistic team Kelly Cox and Eric Mullis, who have been making work together for decades since meeting on a high school ceramics field trip in Wisconsin. Now based in Boise, Idaho, the two build environments that sit somewhere between architecture, product display, and psychic space — treating the built world's mythologies, from retail staging to civic monuments, as material to be dismantled and reassembled.

The installation reportedly works through a vocabulary of symbols without fixed answers, favoring sensation over explanation. That approach fits Monte Vista Projects' identity as one of the Arts District's longest-running artist-run project spaces — a program of Fulcrum Arts' EMERGE initiative that has consistently made room for experimental, non-commercial installation work that bigger galleries tend to avoid.

Given the collaborative duo's description of the work as responding to "persistent violence and misinformation," expect an installation that's more atmospheric and symbol-laden than didactic — worth the trip for anyone interested in how two people build a single visual language across a decades-long creative partnership.

spans.text: That approach fits Monte Vista Projects' identity as one of the Arts District's longest-running artist-run project spaces — a program of Fulcrum Arts' EMERGE initiative that has consistently made room for experimental, non-commercial installation work that bigger galleries tend to avoid.

shows.description:
Galerie Lakaye, a gallery best known for championing Haitian and Caribbean art, pairs two very different painters in this two-person show built around landscape and the natural world. Patrick DeCastro's canvases lean into vivid, saturated color and loosely figured scenes — birds, water, foliage — that sit somewhere between observation and reverie, while Simon Edery's contributions bring a more graphic, patterned sensibility to similar subject matter, breaking the natural world into rhythmic shapes and repeated forms.

Seen together, the two bodies of work read as complementary takes on the same premise: nature not as a backdrop but as a set of colors, patterns, and moods to be reinterpreted on canvas. It's a lighter, warmer summer show for a gallery whose program usually centers on Haitian vodou flags, naive painting, and diasporic art history — a chance to see how that curatorial eye extends to a broader, more international group of contemporary painters.

The gallery itself is worth the visit independent of any single show — its walls are lined year-round with major figures in Haitian modernism (Prefete Duffaut, Wilson Bigaud, Stivenson Magloire) alongside vodou flags and folk art, so a trip to see DeCastro and Edery doubles as an introduction to one of LA's more specialized and least-visited collections.

shows.description:
Durden and Ray is an artist-run collective that has been mounting tightly curated group shows out of its space in the Bendix Building since 2009, and this exhibition is the third chapter of an ongoing painting exchange linking artists across London, Yorkshire, New York, Memphis, and now Los Angeles. Curated by Robert Melzmuf, Christopher Blyth, Karl Bielik, and Rob Hall, it gathers 46 painters whose work ranges from loose, gestural abstraction to tightly structured composition.

The through-line isn't a shared style but a shared commitment to painting as a live, cross-border conversation — each iteration of "The Shadow Side of Everything" has added new cities and new participants, and this LA leg treats the gallery's walls less like a finished statement than a snapshot of an evolving network of studios. For anyone curious about how a scrappy, artist-run space keeps generating international connections without a big institutional budget, it's a useful and rewarding show to walk through.

shows.description:
Earth Elements: Paint and Fire, curated by painter Gary Brewer, sets out to catch a group of established painters in the act of switching mediums. Every artist on the checklist has spent years at the easel before turning to clay, and the show is built around what happens to a painter's instincts once color and gesture have to survive a kiln. Expect glazed surfaces that read like brushwork, lumpy forms that behave like still lifes, and a general disregard for the old high-craft rules that used to separate "ceramics" from "art."

The premise leans on real art history — the show's own framing traces a line from George Ohr and Peter Voulkos's studio-pottery rebellion through the Bay Area funk-ceramics arguments of the 1970s that Brewer lived through firsthand, up to painters today who treat clay as just another canvas. Cybele Rowe and Galia Linn, both long associated with large-scale ceramic sculpture, anchor that conversation from the sculpture side, while Roger Herman, Brad Eberhard, Cheyann Washington and the rest arrive as painters testing the material for the first time or the tenth.

It's a gallery known for community-minded, artist-heavy group shows in a converted industrial space in Lincoln Heights, and this one continues that pattern — eleven artists, one curatorial thesis, and a lot of room to see how differently people handle the same physical constraints. Worth a visit for anyone curious about the current cross-traffic between painting and clay in Los Angeles.

spans.text: It's a gallery known for community-minded, artist-heavy group shows in a converted industrial space in Lincoln Heights, and this one continues that pattern

shows.description:
Faidra Koutsouri, who works under the moniker Ghost Girl, fills 7811 Gallery's Melrose Avenue storefront with paintings and mixed-media pieces that treat memory and mental health as a shared, almost tactile terrain. The show's subtitle, "Are You Mental?", signals the frankness of her approach: rather than softening difficult psychological territory into metaphor, Koutsouri renders it in raw, diaristic imagery — dreamlike scenes, fragmented figures, and soft, bruised color that reads as both vulnerable and defiant.

The paintings on view move between intimate self-portraiture and looser, more symbolic compositions, suggesting an artist working through personal history in real time on the canvas. It's the kind of show that rewards slow looking; details that seem decorative at first glance often carry a harder emotional charge once you spend a few minutes with them.

7811 Gallery has built its identity around exactly this sort of unvarnished, community-facing programming — giving emerging and mid-career Los Angeles artists a low-key storefront platform rather than a white-cube remove. Koutsouri's exhibition fits that mission well, offering an unguarded look at how one artist has translated private struggle into a public body of work.

spans.text: 7811 Gallery has built its identity around exactly this sort of unvarnished, community-facing programming — giving emerging and mid-career Los Angeles artists a low-key storefront platform rather than a white-cube remove.

shows.description:
Scott Hove is best known around Los Angeles for "Cakeland," his long-running walk-in installation of frosting-slathered, faux-confectionary environments that turn sugary kitsch into something a little sinister. For this solo show at La Luz de Jesus, he trades cake stands for clockwork, building a body of new sculptural and wall-based work out of clock faces, gears, and timepiece fragments. The pieces use the familiar iconography of timekeeping to needle at bigger questions about whether time is really the fixed, linear thing we treat it as, or something more slippery.

It's a fitting subject for an artist who has spent his career splicing together things that don't belong side by side — candy-shop cuteness with body horror, mechanical precision with entropy. Expect dense, layered constructions where actual clock parts get embedded in sculpted, cake-like or organic forms, so that the works read simultaneously as functional-looking objects and as reliquaries for a concept (time) that Hove clearly doesn't fully trust.

The show runs alongside two other solo presentations opening the same night at La Luz de Jesus — this Hollywood gallery has been a home base for pop-surrealist and lowbrow art since 1986, and its first-Friday openings remain one of the more reliable draws on the LA gallery circuit. Hove's clock-crammed constructions should be a good anchor for an evening that also includes new work from Wini Brewer and Susie Ketchum.

spans.text: this Hollywood gallery has been a home base for pop-surrealist and lowbrow art since 1986, and its first-Friday openings remain one of the more reliable draws on the LA gallery circuit

shows.description:
This is the first exhibition anywhere dedicated to Bong Joon Ho, and it's built on real access — the museum drew on his personal archive for storyboards, research materials, concept art, creature models, props, and on-set photographs spanning his career from early short films through The Host, Snowpiercer, Okja, and the Oscar-sweeping Parasite. It's a filmmaker's process laid bare rather than a highlight reel: sketches next to the finished monster, notes next to the shot.

What comes through is how consistent Bong's obsessions are across wildly different genres — class conflict, environmental catastrophe, and ordinary people pushed into absurd, often darkly funny situations. Seeing the concept art for Okja's genetically engineered superpig next to production stills from Parasite's flood-lit stairwell makes the throughline of his visual thinking unusually legible.

Curated by Michelle Puetz with Nicholas Barlow, the show continues the museum's Director's Inspiration series (previously spotlighting Agnès Varda) and is a must for anyone who wants to understand how a director who moves fluidly between creature features and social satire actually builds a film from the ground up.

spans.text: continues the museum's Director's Inspiration series (previously spotlighting Agnès Varda)

shows.description:
In the 1980s, Nicolae Ceaușescu's "systematization" campaign flattened roughly a third of historic Bucharest to make way for the oversized avenues and government buildings of a totalitarian regime. Seven churches, deemed too significant to destroy outright, were instead jacked up, set on rails, and physically wheeled behind new apartment blocks — hidden in plain sight rather than demolished. Photographer Anton Roland Laub, who grew up amid this leveled cityscape, spent years tracking down these displaced structures and documenting how they sit today, wedged into gaps between mismatched postwar architecture.

The exhibition — Laub's first solo presentation in the United States — pairs his contemporary large-format photographs with archival material from the era of the relocations, including material from the engineer who devised the rail-lifting technique. The pictures are quiet and procedural rather than sensational: facades caught at odd angles against concrete housing, empty lots where history was erased, buildings that look stranded rather than saved. Together they form a document of a strange, little-known act of architectural survival under one of Eastern Europe's most destructive dictatorships.

This is the first chapter of a three-part project by Laub examining the final years of the Ceaușescu regime, continued in his later series Last Christmas (of Ceaușescu) and Mineriada. Guest-curated by independent curator Sonia Voss, the show fits naturally within the Wende's broader mission of examining Cold War-era Eastern Bloc history through art and archival material, and it rewards a slow look at how state power reshapes — and sometimes just relocates — the physical fabric of a city.

spans.text: the show fits naturally within the Wende's broader mission of examining Cold War-era Eastern Bloc history through art and archival material

shows.description:
Michael Flechtner has spent decades pushing neon past its signage roots into full sculptural territory, and this survey at the Museum of Neon Art gathers work spanning that career. Flechtner came up learning the trade in a six-week bending class in Kansas before moving to Los Angeles to work commercial neon by day and his own sculptures by night, and that hybrid background shows in the work: pieces that use the vocabulary of signage — bent glass tubing, buzzing color, graphic punch — but bend it toward visual puns and conceptual play rather than advertising.

The show's title, "Ecce Artifex" ("Behold the Craftsman"), answers his 1991 MONA solo debut "Ecce Signum" ("Behold the Sign"), and the pairing frames this as a kind of career-spanning victory lap for an artist who has quietly shaped how the medium is treated as art rather than commerce. Flechtner is also the fabricator behind neon elements in works by artists like Bruce Nauman, Doug Aitken, and Betye Saar, so this is also a rare chance to see his own authorial voice front and center rather than in service of someone else's piece.

MONA is the only accredited museum in the U.S. dedicated to neon and electric art, housed in a storefront space in Glendale, and its holdings run from vintage commercial signage to contemporary light-based sculpture. Flechtner's show anchors the museum's current run of exhibitions and is worth catching before it closes in late September.

spans.text: MONA is the only accredited museum in the U.S. dedicated to neon and electric art, housed in a storefront space in Glendale, and its holdings run from vintage commercial signage to contemporary light-based sculpture.

shows.description:
Two Los Angeles painters and life partners share a gallery for an exhibition built around the idea of the Sabbath as, in Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel's phrase, "a palace in time." Robert Russell contributes softly rendered still lifes of Jewish ritual objects — Kiddush cups, yahrzeit candles — painted with a hazy, almost dissolving touch that turns ordinary domestic objects into vessels of memory and quiet loss.

Lisa Edelstein works from her own family photo archive, reconstructing scenes of 1970s suburban New Jersey Jewish life: crowded multigenerational gatherings, patterned wallpaper and furniture, small unposed moments of touch and affection. Her palette and subject matter read as warmer and more anecdotal than Russell's, and the pairing of the two bodies of work sets an intimate, personal register against a more symbolic, object-based one.

Together the two painters build a meditation on ritual, domestic time, and inherited memory — what gets held onto materially versus what only survives as recollection. It's a modestly scaled, human-sized show, well suited to the Skirball's mission of connecting Jewish tradition to broader questions of family and belonging, and it closes the same week as the museum's punk exhibition, so it's worth pairing on one visit.

spans.text: well suited to the Skirball's mission of connecting Jewish tradition to broader questions of family and belonging

shows.description:
Hiva Alizadeh takes her title from Jiroft, the southeastern Iranian archaeological site whose Bronze Age carved chlorite vessels rank among the oldest surviving examples of figurative art from the Iranian plateau. Working across painting and mixed media, Alizadeh translates that ancient visual vocabulary — spiraling florals, animal-headed motifs, dense surface patterning — into a contemporary register, treating the millennia-old carvings less as archaeology than as a living design language still available to draw from.

The paintings on view lean into saturated color and stylized botanical forms, suggesting gardens that are as much invented as remembered. There's a diaristic, almost devotional quality to the repetition of blooms and vines across the canvases, as if the artist is working through a personal iconography built from a shared cultural memory rather than direct observation.

For a gallery devoted largely to Iranian and diasporic artists, the show is a fitting anchor: it treats a deep national history not as a fixed heritage to be illustrated but as material to be reactivated in paint. It's worth seeing alongside the two solo shows opening the same week at Gallery One, which round out a fuller picture of how different Iranian-American women artists are handling questions of memory, myth, and inheritance right now.

spans.text: For a gallery devoted largely to Iranian and diasporic artists

shows.description:
This send-off show gathers six recent graduates of an LA arts high school who've spent years crossing paths at each other's shows, gigs, and film shoots — scoring one another's movies, photographing one another's bands, modeling one another's clothes. Painting, photography, animation, and mixed media all show up here, tied together less by a curatorial thesis than by the fact that everyone in the room has been each other's audience and collaborator for years.

Junior High has built its whole identity around exactly this kind of grassroots, peer-driven programming, and this show captures that spirit at a bittersweet moment: several of the artists are leaving Los Angeles just as the show closes. Expect work that's rougher and more personal than a typical gallery show, dealing openly with community, heartbreak, and the anxiety of growing up in a hostile world, with a closing-night musical send-off from two of the artists' bands.

spans.text: Junior High has built its whole identity around exactly this kind of grassroots, peer-driven programming

shows.description:
GOBI is a small curatorial project space on Madison Avenue devoted to artists, designers, and cultural producers connected to Korea and its diaspora in Los Angeles, and its current show gives Ruoyi Shi a solo platform. "Follow the Feather" leans into the gallery's interest in objects that sit between art and function — the space takes its own name from a Joseon-era Korean cabinet prized equally for beauty and use — and Shi's work continues that conversation between material, craft, and image.

Based on the installation photos, the show favors a light, airy hang with sculptural and wall-based pieces that play with fragility and motion, fitting the exhibition's avian title. It's a good excuse to check out GOBI itself, a project space quietly building one of the more distinctive rosters of Korean and Korean-diaspora artists working in LA today.

Admission is free and the gallery keeps a tight, changing roster of shows, so catching "Follow the Feather" before it closes in late September is worthwhile for anyone interested in emerging sculpture and object-based practice.

shows.description:
Carroll Dunham has spent five decades building one of contemporary painting's most instantly recognizable vocabularies — biomorphic forms, cartoonish anatomy, and hot, unmixed color pushed to the edge of abstraction — and this show at Matthew Brown's Seward Street space brings a new body of paintings, including works from his ongoing "Sharing Space" series glimpsed in the gallery's promotional image.

Dunham emerged from the downtown New York scene of the 1980s and has remained one of the most influential painters of his generation for younger figurative and abstract painters alike; his work moves fluidly between grotesque comedy and formal rigor, often mining the human body — especially figures rendered with exaggerated, almost violent simplicity — for both humor and unease.

This is a rare opportunity to see a major senior American painter's new work on the West Coast, in a gallery that has built its program around exactly this kind of connection between blue-chip figures and the younger artists they've influenced.

spans.text: in a gallery that has built its program around exactly this kind of connection between blue-chip figures and the younger artists they've influenced

shows.description:
Nick Herman has spent two decades making sculpture, photography, and books that treat industrial materials and structural systems as raw poetic material — fat solids cast into a lunar-looking frieze, hand-tied nets that sag under their own logic, antennas that double as myth machines. Museum of Commerce, his solo turn at FOYER-LA titled GREMLIN, promises more of that same sleight of hand: taking the leftover vocabulary of manufacturing, retail, and technology and bending it toward something stranger and more bodily.

FOYER-LA is exactly the kind of space this work needs. Founded by artist Connie Walsh in 2019, it operates out of an in-between space — behind a courtyard, in front of a working studio — built for short, dense, experimental projects rather than white-cube spectacle. Herman's MFA is in sculpture from Yale, and his exhibition history runs through Socrates Sculpture Park, LAXART, and the Chinati Foundation's collection, so a project-space outing lets him work at a scale and speed that bigger institutions don't allow.

Given the title's nod to commerce and gremlins alike, expect a show that pokes at consumer culture and the "traumatic residue" — Herman's own phrase — that industry and technology leave on both land and body. It's a compact, single-artist project, which makes it an easy, quick stop for anyone curious about one of LA's more understated sculptor-writers.

spans.text: Founded by artist Connie Walsh in 2019, it operates out of an in-between space — behind a courtyard, in front of a working studio — built for short, dense, experimental projects rather than white-cube spectacle.

shows.description:
Nonaka-Hill gathers twelve Japanese women artists — among them Atsuko Tanaka, Rei Kawakubo, Kazuko Miyamoto, Tomie Ohtake and Kay Sekimachi — who each, at some point across six decades, worked in a hard-edged, geometric vocabulary that had little patience for softness or sentiment. The show spans painting, sculpture, textile, performance documentation and photography, and its animating idea is straightforward but rarely stated this plainly: that rigor and coolness were themselves a form of resistance for these artists, a way of working against the expressive, macho postures that dominated so much postwar art criticism.

Several of the artists included — Eiko Yamazawa, Aiko Miyawaki, Etsuko Nakatsuji, Shizuko Yoshikawa — also worked as graphic designers, and the show argues that this dual practice sharpened rather than diluted their formal thinking, feeding a shared interest in order and non-psychological composition. It's a smart curatorial premise for a gallery that has spent years building a reputation for surfacing Japanese artists who never got proper due in the U.S., and pairing canonical names like Tanaka with far less exhibited figures like Sumie Aoki and Akiko Horio should make for a genuinely instructive walk through twentieth-century Japanese abstraction.

spans.text: It's a smart curatorial premise for a gallery that has spent years building a reputation for surfacing Japanese artists who never got proper due in the U.S.

shows.description:
Marley Freeman builds her paintings the way a weaver builds cloth: layer by layer, thread of color over thread of color, until an image emerges that feels less composed than grown. For "worthless serpentine," her latest solo show at Parker Gallery, she brings a new group of canvases that continue her long study of abstraction rooted in the structure of textiles — warp and weft translated into hand-mixed gesso and shifting fields of oil and acrylic.

Freeman's forms hover at the edge of recognition: biomorphic shapes, loose grids, and soft-edged color blocks that seem to pulse against one another rather than sit still. The paintings reward slow looking, the kind you'd give a piece of fabric held up to the light — noticing where colors bleed into their neighbors and where a hard edge suddenly appears. It's intimate, handmade work, made by an artist whose paintings already hang in the collections of LACMA and the Hammer.

Parker Gallery has built its program around underrecognized and historically important West Coast artists, and Freeman — based between New York and Massachusetts but deeply tied to the gallery's history (this is her fourth solo show there since 2018) — fits that mission as a contemporary anchor alongside the gallery's roster of overlooked mid-century Californians. This show is a good chance to see how her work has evolved since her last outing here in 2023.

spans.text: Parker Gallery has built its program around underrecognized and historically important West Coast artists
fits that mission as a contemporary anchor alongside the gallery's roster of overlooked mid-century Californians

shows.description:
Paolo Ventura builds miniature worlds and then photographs them as though they were full-scale film sets, and A Human Pace finds him turning that method toward Paris. His pictures conjure a city suspended between memory and invention: deserted streets, lone figures under streetlamps, and interiors that feel like stage sets abandoned mid-scene. The mood is melancholic and theatrical rather than documentary — this is a Paris assembled from nostalgia and imagination as much as from observation.

The show is presented jointly by Galerie XII, the Paris-based photography gallery's Los Angeles branch, and Peter Fetterman Gallery, marking a new collaboration between the two Bergamot Station spaces. Ventura, an Italian photographer known for meticulously constructed dioramas populated with handmade figures, has built a career on blurring the line between staged fiction and lived history, and this body of work continues that practice at a more intimate, human scale.

For viewers who know Ventura's earlier war-haunted tableaux, A Human Pace is a gentler register — closer to reverie than reckoning — but it retains his signature patience: every shadow and prop placed with the deliberateness of a diorama-builder rather than a street photographer.

spans.text: The show is presented jointly by Galerie XII, the Paris-based photography gallery's Los Angeles branch, and Peter Fetterman Gallery, marking a new collaboration between the two Bergamot Station spaces.

shows.description:
Von Wolfe's paintings stage a menagerie of animals — crocodiles, night creatures, watchful predators — rendered in rich, glossy oil on canvas that gives even a small study the weight of a history painting. "Familiars" brings together new canvases ranging from an intimate 55 x 55 cm close-up to a large 180 x 180 cm centerpiece, "Night Visitor," suggesting a show built around scale as much as subject.

There's a storybook menace to the work: animals rendered with enough anatomical specificity to feel real, but staged and lit like symbols or omens rather than straightforward wildlife studies. It fits comfortably within Richard Heller Gallery's roster of narrative, character-driven painters — a program that has long championed figuration with a pop and outsider-art sensibility. For anyone who likes their painting a little uncanny, this is a tightly focused, visually punchy show.

spans.text: It fits comfortably within Richard Heller Gallery's roster of narrative, character-driven painters — a program that has long championed figuration with a pop and outsider-art sensibility.

shows.description:
In 1986, on assignment for the documentary project "A Day in the Life of America," the great Mexican photographer Graciela Iturbide spent a day in a Boyle Heights household connected to the White Fence gang, one of East LA's oldest and most storied. What began as a brief assignment turned into an ongoing relationship that Iturbide returned to over more than three decades; this exhibition presents the photographs from that first 1986 visit, many never widely exhibited.

The pictures are notable for what they don't do: rather than sensationalizing gang life, Iturbide's black-and-white images register tenderness, domesticity and communal bonds, complicated by the fact that many of her subjects, including Rosario, Liza and Cristina, were Deaf as a result of the mid-1960s rubella epidemic and communicated through sign language — hand gestures that can look like coded signs but are, in fact, ordinary conversation.

Iturbide is one of the most significant documentary photographers of the past half-century, and ROSEGALLERY has been a longtime champion of her work within its deep program of 20th- and 21st-century photography. This show is a chance to see a tightly focused, historically rich body of work that treats a stigmatized Los Angeles community with unusual patience and respect.

spans.text: ROSEGALLERY has been a longtime champion of her work within its deep program of 20th- and 21st-century photography

shows.description:
Lara Kempke (also known professionally as Lara Eve Kempke) paints animals as if they were emissaries from another register of experience — birds, big cats and other creatures rendered in layered, richly textured mixed media that leans toward the mystical rather than the naturalistic. A Southern California artist with a background in fashion design, she brings a maximalist, pattern-driven sensibility to her canvases, building up surfaces with paint, collage and gilding until the animal subjects feel iconic, almost devotional.

"Spiritus Animales" (spirit animals) gathers this body of work at bG Gallery's Bergamot Station space. Expect vividly colored, densely worked compositions where a peacock, raven or big cat becomes a kind of totem — a stand-in for instinct, intuition, and the parts of ourselves we don't fully control. Kempke has described her practice as deeply intertwined with process and impulse, and that improvisational energy comes through in surfaces that reward close, slow looking.

For a gallery that has built its program around artists who blur the line between folk sincerity and fine-art polish, Kempke's paintings are a good fit: unapologetically decorative, emotionally direct, and easy to enjoy without a lot of art-historical throat-clearing.

spans.text: For a gallery that has built its program around artists who blur the line between folk sincerity and fine-art polish, Kempke's paintings are a good fit

shows.description:
The Fresh Series is Thinkspace's rolling showcase for Los Angeles-based artists, giving early-career and locally rooted creatives a rotating slot in the gallery's exhibition calendar alongside its bigger solo shows. Session Seventeen brings together three artists — Ella-V-Ella, Juliette Toma, and Daisy Murray — for a group presentation of new work.

As with prior Fresh installments, the show functions as a snapshot of the current local scene rather than a single unified theme, letting each artist's individual approach stand on its own within a shared gallery space.

It opens September 12 with a joint reception alongside the gallery's other new September exhibitions, making for a full night of openings at the West Adams space.

spans.text: The Fresh Series is Thinkspace's rolling showcase for Los Angeles-based artists, giving early-career and locally rooted creatives a rotating slot in the gallery's exhibition calendar alongside its bigger solo shows.

shows.description:
German photographer Ursula Schulz-Dornburg has spent decades documenting landscape and architecture at the edges of political and historical memory, and this show returns to some of her earliest sustained work: black-and-white photographs made in Pagan (Bagan), Burma between 1976 and 1978. The ancient temple field, one of the world's great concentrations of Buddhist monuments, becomes in her hands less a tourist monument than a study in erosion, silence, and scale.

Gallery Luisotti has long championed Schulz-Dornburg's spare, unsentimental eye alongside a roster of landscape and documentary photographers (John Divola, Mark Ruwedel, Lewis Baltz among them), and these Pagan pictures — made decades before her better-known Cold War and Middle East bodies of work — show the same patient attention to structures left to time and weather. It's a quiet show, built for looking slowly.

spans.text: Gallery Luisotti has long championed Schulz-Dornburg's spare, unsentimental eye alongside a roster of landscape and documentary photographers (John Divola, Mark Ruwedel, Lewis Baltz among them)

shows.description:
La Luz de Jesus marks four decades in business with a two-part anniversary exhibition, split into back-to-back installments each with its own opening reception. Since opening in 1986 inside the Soap Plant/Wacko complex on Hollywood Boulevard, the gallery has been credited with helping name and define Pop Surrealism and lowbrow art, launching or championing artists who built careers outside the traditional fine-art gallery circuit.

Given the milestone, expect the anniversary show to function as something of a highlight reel — likely drawing on the gallery's deep artist roster and past exhibition history rather than presenting a single new body of work. The two-part structure (with a changeover and second opening in early November) suggests a rotating cast of contributors across the eight-week run.

For longtime followers of the lowbrow and pop-surrealist scenes, this is a rare chance to see the gallery reflect on its own history in real time, with two separate opening nights to catch different configurations of the show.

spans.text: Since opening in 1986 inside the Soap Plant/Wacko complex on Hollywood Boulevard, the gallery has been credited with helping name and define Pop Surrealism and lowbrow art, launching or championing artists who built careers outside the traditional fine-art gallery circuit.

shows.description:
This is a focused historical survey of the earliest, most experimental years of Keith Sonnier's career, honing in on 1968 to 1970, when the Louisiana-born artist first began bending neon and argon gas into sculpture. Sonnier, who died in 2020, is remembered as one of the great postwar American sculptors, and this show captures the moment he found his signature material: glowing tube light paired with the raw fixtures, transformers, and wiring that power it. Works like the two-tone "Arced Neon" pieces from 1968 show him testing single gestures in colored light, while the later, more elaborate "Neon Wrapping Incandescent V" (1970) shows a fast-maturing vocabulary of layered, multicolor form.

What makes this body of work compelling beyond its historical importance is how physical it still feels — these are sculptures that depend on their walls and corners the way a painting depends on its stretcher bars, casting shadow and colored light into the room and implicating the viewer's own silhouette in the composition. Sonnier arrived at these ideas while still a student, in dialogue with contemporaries like Eva Hesse and Bruce Nauman, and this exhibition (previously shown at the gallery's New York space) makes the case for how radical that dialogue with industrial materials and immaterial light really was.

It's a tightly scoped, jewel-box kind of show rather than a full retrospective, but for anyone interested in postminimalism, the history of light as sculptural material, or just wanting to see real neon glow in person, it's worth the visit.

spans.text: previously shown at the gallery's New York space

shows.description:
Ramiro Hernandez paints in a soft-focus, technicolor haze that reads at once as nostalgic and unsettling — sun-bleached beach scenes hang beside images of weaponry and police equipment, all rendered in the same hazy, Richter-adjacent glow. The Oakland-based painter takes his exhibition's title from Itzhak Bentov's 1977 book on consciousness and holograms, using the idea that "every ripple can mechanically be traced back to the source" as a loose organizing metaphor for a body of work that moves between violence and calm without much visual distinction between the two.

It's a show about how images flatten difference: an idyllic day at the beach and a piece of military hardware can occupy the same fuzzy, sentimental register once they're run through Hernandez's palette. He's showing recently at galleries like Massey Klein and Harkawik in New York and BOZOMAG in LA — this is his first solo outing at Dominique Porter, a small project space in Glassell Park focused on emerging and mid-career painters.

spans.text: a small project space in Glassell Park focused on emerging and mid-career painters

shows.description:
Henri Paul Broyard's second solo show with Tyler Park Presents also marks the gallery's move into its new Melrose Hill location, and it's built around a single, deceptively narrow idea: painting flowers and houseplants entirely in black. Broyard has circled floral still life throughout his career but always avoided the genre's cozy, domestic connotations; rendering the plants in black strips out the sentimentality and turns them into graphic, almost architectural silhouettes that hover between the viewer and a richly colored ground.

The paintings build outward from total abstraction — blocks of color, stripes, grids — before Broyard lets figuration emerge, and he'll sometimes paint back over a resolved image to return it to abstraction, leaving traces of the erased picture underneath. Alongside the paintings, the show continues his series of repaired terracotta and Bauer pots, mended with construction adhesive and metal brackets in a blunt, American riff on kintsugi — vessels that stay visibly broken even as they're made whole again.

Broyard, a Los Angeles native trained at CCA and in Peter Doig's class at Düsseldorf's Kunstakademie, has shown at 12.26 in Dallas, Post Gallery in Zurich and Foreland in the Catskills; his work sits in the collections of the Portland Museum of Art and the California African American Museum.

spans.text: also marks the gallery's move into its new Melrose Hill location

shows.description:
Rafael Megall's paintings work a rich, jewel-toned register somewhere between religious icon and botanical still life, with figures and floral motifs rendered in the flattened, gilded planes of devotional art. Idols In Bloom leans into that vocabulary directly, pairing the language of veneration with the fragility and excess of flowers in full bloom — worship and decay held in the same frame.

Mek Contemporary is a small Glendale gallery with a program built around figuration and craft-forward painting, and this show looks to be a good showcase for Megall's particular fusion of the sacred and the decorative, ornate surfaces built up with the patience of an icon painter but aimed at very contemporary anxieties about beauty and impermanence.

spans.text: Mek Contemporary is a small Glendale gallery with a program built around figuration and craft-forward painting

shows.description:
Devin Flynn has spent decades in the margins between disciplines — as an animation director behind the web series Y'all So Stupid, as the bassist in the band Pixeltan, and as a longtime collaborator of underground comics figure Gary Panter. REALMS is his most defined gallery presentation yet, pulling together years of drawing, collage, and mixed-media work into a survey that traces how his visual language has developed alongside his music and animation careers rather than separately from them.

The show's centerpiece is a new series called OTOFORMS, which folds a literal sound element into the work — a fitting move for an artist whose visual and musical practices have always been intertwined. MutMuz is supplementing the new pieces with a survey of earlier works on paper, posters, prints, and drawings upstairs, plus a program of animation screenings running throughout the exhibition, so visitors get both the new focused body of work and the decades of drawing that led up to it.

Flynn's LA roots run deep: he came up in the city's 1980s graffiti scene under the tag RELM before moving into animation and music, and the show's title nods to that history as much as to the idea of his output existing across separate creative "realms." It's a fitting subject for MutMuz, the Chinatown gallery built out of Mark Mothersbaugh's own archive, which has made a habit of platforming artists whose visual work has lived in the shadow of their music careers.

spans.text: the Chinatown gallery built out of Mark Mothersbaugh's own archive
which has made a habit of platforming artists whose visual work has lived in the shadow of their music careers

shows.description:
Krikor Tchay is a self-taught Armenian-American painter working in mixed media — acrylic and spray paint built up in dense, layered passages that read somewhere between graffiti, abstract expressionism and pop collage. Collective Noise gathers a body of his recent canvases that circle around vulnerability, desire and resilience, using clashing color and gestural mark-making to visualize emotional static: the "noise" of competing feelings that most people carry quietly.

The paintings on view lean into contrast — hard graphic edges next to loose drips, saturated color fields interrupted by scratched-in text and figures — a language Tchay has been refining since his 2018 "Tangled" series. It's unpretentious, autobiographical work made by an artist who has built his following largely through Instagram and word of mouth rather than gallery representation, which makes this extended run at Eye For Sound (a small storefront space run in partnership with a neighborhood coffee shop) a good chance to see a substantial group of his paintings together in person rather than as scattered studio posts.

Eye For Sound itself is worth knowing about: an Eagle Rock gallery founded around the idea of pairing visual art with music, co-run by musician Serj Tankian, that has quickly built a program mixing emerging local painters with music-world photography and memorabilia shows.

spans.text: Eye For Sound itself is worth knowing about: an Eagle Rock gallery founded around the idea of pairing visual art with music, co-run by musician Serj Tankian, that has quickly built a program mixing emerging local painters with music-world photography and memorabilia shows.

shows.description:
Chris Lux is a San Francisco-based painter and collagist known for densely layered canvases that stack figure drawing, comic-book imagery, sculptural elements and even painted architectural fragments into single compositions — sometimes expanding into full painted rooms that swallow the viewer along with the artwork. He has been showing steadily since 2008, including an earlier immersive installation, Absinthe, that turned an entire gallery room into one continuous painted environment.

This solo show at GGLA (Guerrero Gallery's Los Angeles outpost in Glassell Park) brings his layered, referential style to the gallery's Verdugo Road storefront. Expect the same interest in "portals to the past" that defines his practice: images and tiles of imagery — drawn from history, literature and pop culture — arranged so the eye is constantly renegotiating what it's looking at, a painting inside a painting inside a studio.

GGLA has built a steady roster of solo shows in this Glassell Park space through 2026, and Lux's exhibition continues that program with an artist whose work rewards slow, close looking rather than a quick glance.

spans.text: GGLA has built a steady roster of solo shows in this Glassell Park space through 2026

shows.description:
This two-person exhibition pairs Darren Cortez, whose paintings often traffic in gothic, folkloric imagery — crows, blades, ritual objects rendered with a graphic, tattoo-flash intensity — with Tanya Brodsky, an LA sculptor who reworks found urban hardware (security bars, bed frames, rolling gates) into wry, body-conscious objects. Both artists share an interest in taking materials loaded with menace or utility and bending them toward something stranger: Cortez through image-making steeped in memento-mori symbolism, Brodsky through a sculptural practice that sandblasts and re-chromes the architecture of domestic security into objects that read as almost tender.

Brodsky, who was born in Kyiv and trained at RISD and UC San Diego, has spent years mining the visual language of window bars and fences — devices meant to keep bodies out or in — and turning them into sculptures that flirt with humor, vulnerability, and camp; her public commission "Yolki Palki" carried that same colorful, industrial-materials sensibility into a West Hollywood streetscape. Cortez's paintings, seen in NOON's recent group shows, favor a stark, illustrative style that draws on tattoo culture and outlaw iconography.

Pairing the two suggests a show interested in toughness as a surface that can be cut into, softened, or reclaimed — appropriate for a Chinatown project space that has built its program around artists working through spirituality, craft, and the body. Expect a mix of wall-based painting and object-sculpture that plays off each other's hard materials and soft undertones.

spans.text: appropriate for a Chinatown project space that has built its program around artists working through spirituality, craft, and the body

shows.description:
Michel Auder has spent more than sixty years pointing a camera at whatever was in front of him — friends, lovers, hotel rooms, television screens, the inside of his own apartment — and this show pulls together the photographic side of that restless archive. Auder was one of the first artists to treat portable video as a real medium rather than a novelty, and the black-and-white and color photographs here function less like discrete artworks than like frames pulled out of a much longer continuous take. Alongside the stills, moving-image works extend the same logic into time.

It's a fitting inaugural show for Jeni Abramson Gallery, a new Los Angeles program devoted to photography, multimedia, and conceptual art. Auder's decades of documenting Warhol-era downtown New York (he crossed paths with Alice Neel, Cindy Sherman, Hannah Wilke, and Larry Rivers, among others) give the work a specific historical weight, but the images on view are presented as an open-ended visual archive rather than a greatest-hits survey — records of looking as much as records of who was in the room.

The exhibition is accompanied by a book of the same title, treated as an extension of the show rather than a catalogue afterthought, with tactile photographs on the wall placed in dialogue with the printed page. Opening day includes a 3pm conversation between Auder and curator Hamza Walker, followed by a reception — a strong way to launch a gallery clearly aiming for serious, artist-driven programming rather than safe crowd-pleasers.

spans.text: It's a fitting inaugural show for Jeni Abramson Gallery, a new Los Angeles program devoted to photography, multimedia, and conceptual art.
a strong way to launch a gallery clearly aiming for serious, artist-driven programming rather than safe crowd-pleasers

shows.description:
Jonathan Ryan takes his exhibition's title from a line in Steinbeck's Cannery Row describing the hush of early morning before the sun rises — a threshold moment between night and day that becomes the show's governing mood. Ryan, a Buffalo-born, LA-based painter with an MFA from Tyler School of Art, has built a body of work around exactly these liminal states: light that hasn't decided what it is yet, figures caught in transitional interiors, the strange clarity that appears right before ordinary vision resumes.

Ryan's paintings tend to work in hazy, saturated color and soft-edged forms, giving even mundane domestic scenes an charged, almost hallucinatory quality. He has shown previously at the Landing in LA and Hesse Flatow in New York, and was recently included in a group show at the Utah Museum of Contemporary Art, signaling a painter whose quiet, atmospheric canvases are gaining wider institutional notice.

This is one of three concurrent solo presentations opening the same week at Megan Mulrooney's Santa Monica Boulevard space — part of the gallery's format of running two to three shows in parallel across its rooms, encouraging viewers to move between distinct sensibilities in a single visit.

spans.text: part of the gallery's format of running two to three shows in parallel across its rooms, encouraging viewers to move between distinct sensibilities in a single visit.

shows.description:
Omaha-based painter Falon Stutzman returns to Megan Mulrooney following her 2025 debut solo show there, Woman Having a Hard Time, which introduced her flattened, cartoon-inflected figures caught in states of quiet emotional overload — waiting tables, curled up with a dog, stalled mid-gesture. The End of a Long Line looks to continue that project of turning everyday female personhood into something both comic and faintly tragic.

Stutzman paints in oil and flashe, building scenes with bruised, queasy color and spatial distortions borrowed from animation and New Wave film stills. Her figures are archetypes rather than portraits — generic enough to be anyone, particular enough to sting. She's a Columbus College of Art and Design graduate whose work has appeared in New American Paintings, and this second LA solo suggests a gallery relationship still very much building momentum.

The show opens alongside two other solos at Megan Mulrooney, part of the gallery's rotating multi-room format on Santa Monica Boulevard.

spans.text: part of the gallery's rotating multi-room format on Santa Monica Boulevard

shows.description:
Ecognosis pairs two artists whose work turns an eye toward the entanglement of body and landscape, human systems and ecological ones. Julia Bennett has built a body of work around scorched and shifting terrain in past shows at this gallery, and here her paintings continue to treat the earth as a live, volatile surface rather than a backdrop. Mary Gortani's contributions lean into more intimate, tactile registers, with surfaces and forms that suggest organic growth, decay, and repair happening in close-up.

Installed in One Trick Pony's small Western Avenue storefront, the show relies on proximity — visitors move through a tight run of paintings and objects that reward slow looking. The title, borrowed from ecological philosophy's notion of "ecognosis" (a felt, embodied awareness of one's entanglement with a larger ecosystem), signals the show's ambition to make viewers physically conscious of interdependence rather than just intellectually aware of it.

It's a fitting project for this scrappy, artist-friendly gallery, which has built a reputation for pairing emerging Los Angeles painters in unexpected two-hander shows. Worth a visit for anyone tracking younger LA painters working through questions of nature, materiality, and site.

shows.description:
Audrey Densmore is an LA-based puppeteer, builder, and illustrator trained at CalArts, known for her work fabricating puppets and props for film and television (including stints associated with the Bob Baker Marionette Theater world and various stop-motion and puppetry productions around town). "People in Movies" is her solo show at Heavy Manners, the Sunset Boulevard lending library, gallery, and bookstore that doubles as a community hub for zines, classes, and small exhibitions.

Given Densmore's background, expect the show to lean into her cinematic and puppetry roots — likely illustration, character studies, or handmade objects that read like stills from movies that don't exist. Heavy Manners' gallery wall is a small, intimate space, well suited to this kind of dense, craft-driven personal work rather than a sprawling installation.

Heavy Manners itself is worth knowing regardless of what's on the walls: part lending library, part indie bookstore, part gallery, it's one of the more unusual project spaces in Echo Park/Silver Lake, threading a packed calendar of figure-drawing nights, risograph workshops, and readings around its rotating exhibitions.
