shows.description:
La Loma's summer group show crams sixteen artists into the small Highland Park gallery, working the seam between comedy and unease. Jake Longstreth contributes his signature deadpan paintings of exurban nowhere-places — strip malls and parking lots rendered with the solemnity of landscape painting. Joe Sola's "Birdhouse" applies his conceptual, deadpan humor to a primary-colored birdhouse painting that pointedly doesn't function as a birdhouse should. Jude Pauli's ceramic totems build their own wobbly internal logic, while Kansas Smeaton's lush, Rococo-tinged paintings recast who gets to be the subject of opulence and desire.

The through-line is a kind of genre-bending mischief: paintings that behave like objects, ceramics that behave like paintings, sculptures that edge into architecture. Ryan Dobrowski's and Cindy Phenix's large canvases anchor the show's more painterly, atmospheric register, while Jared McGriff's cosmologically-scaled figure painting pulls the show toward something more meditative. It's a loose, generous survey rather than a tightly argued thesis show — a good entry point if you want a cross-section of what's happening in LA painting and ceramics right now, from a gallery that's quietly become one of the better project spaces in NELA.

spans.text: from a gallery that's quietly become one of the better project spaces in NELA

shows.description:
Cast Shadows brings together David Vega's large-scale paintings and Andy Montiel Phillips' sculptures around a shared interest in how bright, cartoonish, instantly recognizable imagery can carry darker historical and psychological weight. Vega's paintings draw on vibrant color and crisp graphic patterning to address Indigenous displacement, cultural erasure, and the friction between ancestral identity and imposed religious frameworks.

Montiel Phillips works with a reduced, cartoon-like vocabulary — most notably the white picket fence — to explore nostalgia as both a comforting and politically loaded device, freezing a mid-century American symbol into a flattened, stage-set facade that shifts as the viewer moves around it.

Together the two bodies of work use familiar, almost pop-inflected surfaces as an entry point into questions about who gets to record history and how collective memory distorts over time. It's a fitting continuation of Currency Exchange's mission as a community-embedded gallery in Mid-City, pairing accessible imagery with pointed critique.

spans.text: It's a fitting continuation of Currency Exchange's mission as a community-embedded gallery in Mid-City, pairing accessible imagery with pointed critique.

shows.description:
Jessie Stevenson's first California exhibition gathers new oil paintings made after the London-based artist's inaugural trip to the state, with plein-air sketches done in Ojai, Hollywood, Venice, and San Diego later worked up into finished canvases back in her studio. Stevenson builds her surfaces with an unusual egg-oil-titanium ground that mimics the tooth of a sketchbook page, then layers semi-transparent oil glazes over it — a technique she developed during her fellowship at the Slade School of Fine Art.

The paintings sit at the hinge between British Romantic landscape painting (Constable, Turner) and American traditions of depicting the West, from Bierstadt's grandeur to Agnes Pelton's more mystical visions. Freeway interchanges, coastal bluffs, and chaparral hillsides appear rendered with the same trembling, atmospheric touch Stevenson usually reserves for the English countryside, pushed toward abstraction and inflected by a recurring iridescent blue.

It's a quietly ambitious debut for the gallery's Los Angeles outpost (formerly Sapling in London): a British painter's outsider view of Southern California landscape, filtered through art-historical memory and accompanied by a small poetry publication illustrated with her own sketches and photographs.

spans.text: the gallery's Los Angeles outpost (formerly Sapling in London)

shows.description:
Jinyoung Park's first solo exhibition at Lee & Lee Gallery pairs forty-five small-format photographs with short handwritten texts, all built around the uniform intimacy of an 8-by-10 frame. Park trained in visual design and photography before working in broadcast production, and that background shows in the way these images are staged: quiet, carefully lit glimpses of ordinary domestic moments rather than grand landscapes or portraits.

The through-line is explicitly devotional — Park frames the everyday as evidence of a larger love, and the accompanying texts (in Korean) read like diary entries or prayers rather than didactic captions. It's a modest, sincere body of work that fits the gallery's long-running role as a community space for Korean and Korean-American faith-based art in Koreatown.

Visitors should expect an unassuming, contemplative show best taken slowly — the pleasure here is in the accumulation of small, personal images rather than any single showstopping piece.

spans.text: fits the gallery's long-running role as a community space for Korean and Korean-American faith-based art in Koreatown

shows.description:
Naomi is a suite of drawings by Sophie Roessler centered on a single recurring figure: a dancer at the storied Hollywood dive bar Jumbo's Clown Room. Roessler traces, collages, and reworks the same image obsessively, turning her subject into something between a muse and a mirage — a study in how repeated looking (and repeated digital exposure) shapes desire and identity.

The drawings mix girlish ephemera — swans, bunnies, tattoo flash, airbrushed haze — with the language of parasocial fixation, treating the accumulation of imagery itself as a kind of diary. It's a show about spectatorship as much as it is about the woman being looked at, pulling in ideas from Jungian anima theory and feminist film criticism without ever feeling like an academic exercise.

Leiminspace is one of Chinatown's scrappier, more consistently interesting spaces, known for platforming artists who don't always fit neatly into the gallery mainstream. This solo show is a good example of why it's worth checking in on regularly, even though the space is easy to miss from the street.

shows.description:
Seasons, the small artist-run photography gallery tucked above a Chinatown dispensary and print shop, opens its next exhibition on September 12 with a presentation of work by Malerie Marder. Marder is a Los Angeles-based photographer long associated with the staged, psychologically charged domestic tableaux that emerged from the Yale MFA program in the 1990s alongside artists like Gregory Crewdson and Justine Kurland — work that treats the family photograph and the snapshot's intimacy as a subject for careful, often unsettling reconstruction.

Seasons has not yet published a title, checklist, or statement for the show, which is typical of how the gallery rolls out its program — announcements arrive close to the opening, with fuller details following once the work is installed.

Given Marder's history of exhibiting internationally and the gallery's habit of pairing serious, established photographers with its emerging roster, this is a show worth watching for as the date approaches, even with details still thin.

shows.description:
Activist Artist is an open-air group exhibition on the fence and lot art space SPARC calls SPARCin' LOTS, next to its Venice Blvd headquarters. SPARC invited artists to respond to the 2024 presidential election and the political climate that followed, and the result is a rolling, outdoor salon of protest paintings, prints and mixed-media pieces that gets new additions on an ongoing basis.

The tone is direct and unambiguous: work by Ralph D'Oliveira, Olivia Ramos, Karen Fiorito, Teresa Greve Wolf, FLACO, sandra tamkin, Jason Kartez and Cesar Garcia takes on immigration policy, reproductive rights, police violence and the erosion of democratic norms, often with wall-text statements from the artists themselves explaining what's at stake in each piece. Karen Fiorito's screenprinted portrait of Shirley Chisholm and FLACO's Greco-Roman-inspired mosaic on abortion access are among the standouts.

Because it's outdoors and free to see any time, it functions less like a conventional gallery show and more like a public billboard for dissent — very much in keeping with SPARC's 50-year history of using murals and public art as organizing tools.

spans.text: very much in keeping with SPARC's 50-year history of using murals and public art as organizing tools

shows.description:
Ramon Saturnino's new exhibition at Frankfurt Ordorica takes its title from two seemingly unrelated places — Bulgaria and Mexicali — that the artist yokes together as a way of thinking about the strange logic of borders, migration routes, and the geographic imagination. Rather than a literal travelogue, the show reads as a meditation on how place names circulate as symbols long after their specific histories are forgotten, and how an artist working in Los Angeles might hold two distant, disconnected geographies in mind at once.

Frankfurt Ordorica has built a reputation showing young Los Angeles-based sculptors and painters working through questions of memory, material, and displacement (its recent slate included group shows on modernist housing history and figurative sculpture), and Saturnino's solo outing continues that thread with a body of new work that plays with the tension between the personal and the cartographic.

This is very much a gallery on the rise in the East Hollywood/Western Avenue corridor, worth a visit for anyone tracking where LA's next generation of exhibiting artists first get solo shows.

shows.description:
Ann Leda Shapiro has spent five decades making watercolors and works on paper that treat the body as a landscape of feeling — skin standing in for terrain, internal organs rendered as weather systems, psychological states given physical form. Her paintings move fluidly between the anatomical and the cosmic: a "Bonded Bodies" composition, a smoke-veiled tree at the edge of a fire, a spine drawn like a coiled snake. There's a loose, watery immediacy to her line that owes something to both feminist body art of the 1970s and older traditions of visionary and medical illustration.

"Through the Tunnel" gathers work spanning from the 1970s through her recent wildfire and tree paintings, tracing a long arc in which the personal (illness, aging, grief) keeps bumping up against the environmental (drought, fire, loss of habitat). Titles like "Smoke from Wildfires" and "Tornado" sit alongside earlier, more intimate pieces such as "Intestinal Distress" and "Holding On," suggesting a practice that has always used the body to talk about the world, and vice versa.

For a gallery best known for younger, more conceptually brash programming, giving space to an artist who has been quietly working this vein since the 1970s feels like a corrective — a chance to see how a career built on unguarded, visceral image-making holds up against, and speaks to, the present moment.
